Local protonic gating in
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021046] Published Fri May 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a time-reversal symmetric superconducting diode effect in gate-defined homojunctions using local protonic gating.
motivation: To achieve magnetic-field-free control of nonreciprocal critical currents in superconducting devices.
method: Local protonic gating is applied to homojunctions to induce a superconducting diode effect while preserving time-reversal symmetry.
result: Polarity-tunable, time-reversal symmetric superconducting diode effect is realized, enabling control of nonreciprocal critical currents without magnetic fields.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for superconducting diode effects in homojunctions, with potential applications in superconducting electronics.

title: Elastic And Structural Anisotropy In Silica Thin Films For Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, And Silvia Corezzi
abstract:
Author(s): Brenda Bracco, Michele Magnozzi, Stefano Colace, Maurizio Canepa, Giulio Favaro, Marco Bazzan, Massimo Granata, David Hofman, Alessandro Di Michele, Laura Silenzi, Gianpietro Cagnoli, Giovanni Carlotti, Paola Sassi, and Silvia Corezzi

Researchers find that silica films in mirror coatings of gravitational-wave detectors have hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment. This discovery informs coating design and deposition and postprocessing strategies aimed at reducing thermal noise.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021036] Published Fri May 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies elastic and structural anisotropy in silica thin films used in gravitational-wave detector mirror coatings, focusing on material properties and thermal noise reduction.
motivation: Thermal noise in mirror coatings limits the sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors; understanding and mitigating anisotropy in silica films could improve detector performance.
method: The authors characterize the elastic and structural properties of silica thin films using experimental techniques to detect hidden anisotropy and evaluate the effectiveness of standard heat treatments.
result: Silica films exhibit hidden anisotropy that resists standard heat treatment, informing coating design and postprocessing strategies.
conclusion: The findings guide the development of deposition and postprocessing strategies to reduce thermal noise in gravitational-wave detectors.

title: Colloquium: What Do We Mean By ‘active Matter’?
authors: Michael Te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, And Michael E. Cates
abstract:
Author(s): Michael te Vrugt, Benno Liebchen, and Michael E. Cates

Active matter has become a lively topic in recent years, but what exactly is meant by the term ‘active matter’ is often unclear. This Colloquium discusses the scientific and semantic issues underlying this ambiguity, as well as the history of the field, and offers a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems. It then surveys recent developments including nonreciprocal interactions, intracellular phase separation, and quantum active matter.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 031001] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the definition and scope of active matter as a subset of nonequilibrium systems, including recent developments like nonreciprocal interactions and quantum active matter.
motivation: The term 'active matter' is often used ambiguously; the paper aims to clarify its meaning and provide a precise definition.
method: The authors review the history and current usage of the term, propose a definition, and survey recent developments in the field.
result: They offer a definition of active matter as a well-defined subset of nonequilibrium systems and highlight emerging topics such as quantum active matter.
conclusion: A clear definition helps unify the field and guide future research, but the paper is a review without novel technical contributions to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution using a scanning probe as an optical antenna.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and achieve atomic-scale resolution for studying molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
method: Combines scanning probe microscopy with optical fluorescence, using the tip as a nanoscale optical antenna to confine the electromagnetic field.
result: Achieves superresolution down to the atomic scale, enabling the study of individual molecules and submolecular structures.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy provides new insights into molecular identification and reactions at the atomic scale.

title: Pressure Effects On Metals, Alloys, And Compounds Of Transplutonium Elements
authors: Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, And Thomas E. Albrecht
abstract:
Author(s): Tyler W. Hines, Nicholas B. Beck, Kacy N. Mendoza, Joseph M. Sperling, and Thomas E. Albrecht

Materials containing transplutonium elements (the actinides Am–Cm that come after Pu in the periodic table) are important for nuclear power, nuclear waste management, and long-term storage. They also have fascinating properties, with 5
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics and chemistry of transplutonium compounds under high pressure, focusing on their electronic structure and material properties.
motivation: Transplutonium elements are important for nuclear power and waste management, and their 5f electrons exhibit unique behavior at the boundary of localization and itinerancy.
method: The paper is a review summarizing experimental and theoretical studies of transplutonium metals, alloys, and coordination complexes under high pressure.
result: It highlights the challenges and recent advances in understanding the electronic and structural properties of these radioactive materials.
conclusion: The reviewed work expands our understanding of transplutonium materials but does not directly address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium discusses the prospects for detecting continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and the multimessenger implications.
motivation: Continuous gravitational waves are a key frontier in gravitational-wave astrophysics, with connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics.
method: The paper reviews detection prospects for upcoming gravitational-wave detectors and emphasizes simultaneous electromagnetic observations.
result: It surveys potential implications for understanding physical and astrophysical processes in dense neutron star environments.
conclusion: Multimessenger observations combining gravitational and electromagnetic waves will enhance our understanding of neutron star interiors and related physics.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants based on a least-squares adjustment of all available data.
motivation: Accurate and consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology, requiring periodic updates as new measurements become available.
method: A least-squares adjustment is performed on a global dataset of measurements and theoretical calculations, taking into account correlations and uncertainties.
result: A self-consistent set of values for fundamental constants and conversion factors is provided, with updated uncertainties reflecting the latest data.
conclusion: The 2022 CODATA values represent the most accurate and reliable set of fundamental constants, serving as a standard reference for physics and chemistry.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, covering single-particle and collective behaviors.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment between orientation and velocity leads to novel active matter phenomena.
method: Unified mathematical and conceptual framework, review of existing models.
result: Self-alignment enables orbiting, synchronized motion, and other collective behaviors.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed for biological and clinical insight; optoacoustic imaging offers high-resolution, deep-tissue optical contrast noninvasively.
method: The review covers the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging of optical contrast at millimeter-to-centimeter depths with high resolution, bridging the gap between optical and ultrasound imaging.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical imaging, with ongoing advancements in multimodal approaches enhancing its capabilities.

title: Periodic Gravitational Lensing With Oscillating Boson Stars
authors: Xing-Yu Yang (杨星宇), Tan Chen (陈坦), And Rong-Gen Cai
abstract:
Author(s): Xing-Yu Yang (杨星宇), Tan Chen (陈坦), and Rong-Gen Cai (蔡荣根)

We show that oscillating (real-scalar) boson stars generically host an oscillating radial caustic. Sources near this caustic cross it every half period, thereby producing periodic caustic-crossing lensing. The resulting observables are phase locked to the lens oscillation: image-pair creation or ann…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031403] Published Fri Jul 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies periodic gravitational lensing caused by oscillating boson stars, a topic in astrophysics.
motivation: To explore observable signatures of boson stars, which are hypothetical compact objects, through gravitational lensing.
method: The authors analyze the lensing properties of oscillating real-scalar boson stars, identifying an oscillating radial caustic and computing image-pair creation/annihilation.
result: They find that sources near the caustic produce periodic lensing events phase-locked to the boson star oscillation.
conclusion: Oscillating boson stars can generate unique periodic lensing signals that may be detectable in future observations.

title: Progenitor Of The Recoiling Supermassive Black Hole Rbh-1 Identified Using Hst And Jwst Imaging
authors: Tousif Islam, Tejaswi Venumadhav, And Digvijay Wadekar
abstract:

Using a combination of Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope imaging, a runaway supermassive black hole was recently identified with an inferred velocity of [MATH], likely ejected from a compact star-forming galaxy at…

tldr: This paper identifies the progenitor of a recoiling supermassive black hole using HST and JWST imaging.
motivation: To understand the origin and dynamics of a runaway supermassive black hole candidate.
method: Analysis of multi-wavelength imaging data from HST and JWST to identify the host galaxy and ejection event.
result: The progenitor galaxy and likely ejection mechanism are identified.
conclusion: The study confirms the black hole's recoil origin and provides insights into supermassive black hole dynamics.

title: Extending Ground-Based Gravitational-Wave Sensitivity To 5 Hz
authors: Amit Singh Ubhi, Lari Koponen, Jiri Smetana, Yulin Xia, Haixing Miao, Emilia Chick, John Bryant, Geraint Pratten, Teng Zhang, Richard Mittleman, Peter Fritschel, Alan V. Cumming, Giles Hammond, And Denis Martynov
abstract:

Extending the sensitivity of terrestrial gravitational-wave detectors below 20 Hz is a long-standing challenge, limited by ground motion and inertial sensing noise. In this Letter, we demonstrate ultra-high-vacuum compatible inertial isolation and position sensing technologies that achieve active pl…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031401] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents experimental techniques to extend the sensitivity of ground-based gravitational-wave detectors down to 5 Hz by improving inertial isolation and position sensing.
motivation: Extending gravitational-wave detector sensitivity below 20 Hz is challenging due to ground motion and sensor noise; achieving this would open a new observational window.
method: The authors demonstrate ultra-high-vacuum compatible inertial isolation and position sensing technologies that achieve active platform stabilization at low frequencies.
result: They show that the proposed system can reduce noise and enable sensitivity down to 5 Hz, a significant improvement over current detectors.
conclusion: The demonstrated technologies could be integrated into future gravitational-wave observatories to enhance their low-frequency performance.

title: Crust Glass Formation Reveals The Neutron Star Birth Properties In Igr J17480-2446
authors: D. A. Baiko And A. I. Chugunov
abstract:

IGR J17480-2446 is a low-mass x-ray binary, harboring an exceptional accreting pulsar (a neutron star) with an unusual spin frequency of 11 Hz and a very slow postoutburst crust cooling. The former may imply that it is observed at an early stage of recycling, while the latter was shown to indicate t…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031402] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies crust glass formation in a neutron star to infer its birth properties.
motivation: Understanding the early evolution of neutron stars and the recycling process in low-mass X-ray binaries.
method: Modeling the formation of a glassy crust in the neutron star IGR J17480-2446 and comparing with observed cooling data.
result: The slow postoutburst cooling is explained by crust glass formation, revealing the neutron star's birth spin and age.
conclusion: The neutron star in IGR J17480-2446 is likely young and was born with a slow spin, consistent with early recycling.

title: Anomaly In Canonical Semiclassical Gravity
authors: Viqar Husain And Irfan Javed
abstract:
Author(s): Viqar Husain and Irfan Javed

We show that the canonical formulation of the semiclassical Einstein equation, where the matter terms in the constraints are replaced by expectation values of the corresponding operators in quantum states, is inconsistent due to the nonclosure of the resulting constraint algebra.


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031501] Published Thu Jul 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows an inconsistency in the canonical formulation of semiclassical gravity due to non-closure of the constraint algebra.
motivation: To check the consistency of semiclassical Einstein equations where matter is treated quantum mechanically.
method: Canonical analysis of the constraint algebra in semiclassical gravity.
result: The constraint algebra does not close, indicating inconsistency.
conclusion: The canonical semiclassical approach to gravity is inconsistent.

title: Search For Sub-GeV Dark Particles In $η→{π}^{0}+\text{Invisible}$ Decay

abstract:

tldr: This paper reports an experimental search for a sub-GeV dark scalar particle in η→π^0+invisible decays using BESIII data, finding no signal.

method: The BESIII collaboration analyzed over 10 billion J/ψ events to search for the decay η→π^0+invisible, looking for missing energy signatures.
result: No significant signal was observed, and upper limits on the branching fraction were set.
conclusion: The null result constrains models of sub-GeV dark matter, but does not directly relate to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Dynamical Pathway To Radiative Divertor Driven By Transient X-Point Vortex In Tokamaks
authors: H. Yang, N. Fedorczak, G. Ciraolo, E. Serre, H. Bufferand, L. Fèvre, E. Havlickova, N. Lemoine, N. Rivals, P. Tamain, The WEST Team, And The WPTE Team
abstract:

motivation: Understanding and controlling radiative divertors is crucial for managing heat exhaust in fusion reactors.
method: The authors analyze experimental data from the WEST tokamak and perform numerical simulations to investigate the formation and stability of X-point radiators.
result: They identify a dynamical pathway involving transient X-point vortices that drive the formation of a stable radiative divertor.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into the physics of X-point radiators and may help in developing control strategies for fusion plasmas.

title: Observation Of $cp$ Violation In ${B}^{0}→J/ψρ(770{)}^{0}$ Decays

[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 031803] Published Wed Jul 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports the observation of CP violation in B0→J/ψρ(770)0 decays by the LHCb collaboration.

title: First-Principles Explanation Of The Drift Configuration Dependence Of The Radial Electric Field And High-Confinement Access In Tokamaks
authors: B. J. Frei, R. Bilato, O. Grover, W. Zholobenko, C. Angioni, M. Bergmann, P. Ulbl, F. Jenko, And The ASDEX Upgrade Team
abstract:

The origin of the difference in the high-confinement ([MATH]-mode) power threshold between favorable and unfavorable drift configurations in tokamaks—experimentally linked to a deeper radial electric field ([MATH]) well in the former—remains unresolved. Using first-principles gyrokinetic simulations…

result: Identifies a density-dependent reversal mechanism in bacterial aerotaxis.
conclusion: The work provides insights into collective behavior in living systems but has no connection to quantum information theory or thermodynamics.

title: Lifting Active Matter Into Three Dimensions Using Buoyancy Control And External Alignment
authors: Sandeep Ramteke, Jordan Dehmel, Touvia Miloh, Jarrod Schiffbauer, And Alicia Boymelgreen
abstract:
Author(s): Sandeep Ramteke, Jordan Dehmel, Touvia Miloh, Jarrod Schiffbauer, and Alicia Boymelgreen

Density matching and field-induced alignment are used to suppress sedimentation and gyrotaxis, facilitating sustained three-dimensional transport of electrokinetically driven active colloids in the bulk.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L032005] Published Tue Jul 14, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to lift active colloids into three dimensions using buoyancy control and external alignment, enabling sustained 3D transport.
motivation: Active colloids typically sediment or exhibit gyrotaxis, limiting their motion to 2D. The authors aim to achieve sustained 3D transport for applications in microrobotics and material assembly.
method: Density matching and field-induced alignment are used to suppress sedimentation and gyrotaxis, allowing electrokinetically driven active colloids to move in the bulk.
result: The approach successfully enables three-dimensional transport of active colloids, overcoming previous limitations.
conclusion: This work provides a practical method for 3D control of active matter, with potential applications in targeted delivery and microfluidics.

This work introduces a new class of excitable systems, which extends the well-known FitzHugh-Nagumo model to allow for dynamic variation of the phase sp…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033052] Published Mon Jul 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper models molluscan shell pigmentation patterns using a novel excitable system that extends the FitzHugh-Nagumo model with dynamic phase space variation.
motivation: To understand the mechanisms underlying the diverse pigmentation patterns observed in mollusc shells.
method: The authors introduce a new class of excitable systems that allow for dynamic variation of the phase space, extending the FitzHugh-Nagumo model.
result: The model reproduces a wide range of shell pigmentation patterns, suggesting that dynamic excitability is a key mechanism.
conclusion: Dynamic excitability can explain the diversity of molluscan shell patterns, providing a theoretical framework for pattern formation in biology.

result: They find that the spin polarization of hypertriton can be used to unravel the proton spin polarization, providing insights into the vortical structure of the quark-gluon plasma.
conclusion: Hypertriton production offers a new probe for studying spin polarization in heavy-ion collisions, which may help understand the vortical properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

title: High-energy Emission From The Galactic Center
authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, and Régis Terrier

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy emission from the Galactic Center, covering the supermassive black hole, compact sources, and plasma bubbles.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of the high-energy phenomena in the Galactic Center region.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths, including X-ray and gamma-ray observations.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of the quiescent and flaring emission from Sgr A*, as well as other high-energy sources in the region.
conclusion: The Galactic Center is a unique laboratory for studying high-energy astrophysical processes, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on the role of surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability and efficiency.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights can help improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium decays and new hadron searches.
motivation: Understanding strong interaction mechanisms such as quark confinement and gluon binding through charmonium decays and searches for new hadrons.
method: Review of experimental results from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments on hadron production in e+e- collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs.
result: Summarizes current progress and highlights recent advances from BESIII as the leading facility for such measurements.
conclusion: The study of open-charm meson pairs provides crucial insights into strong interaction dynamics and hadron spectroscopy.

title: Editorial: A Tribute To The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Véronique van Elewyck And Dietrich Belitz
abstract:
Author(s): Véronique Van Elewyck and Dietrich Belitz

Three Colloquia honor the Arecibo Observatory’s legacy, exploring its revolutionary impact on planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.

[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 010001] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: An editorial tribute to the Arecibo Observatory, summarizing its legacy in planetary radar, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
motivation: To honor the Arecibo Observatory's contributions and impact on various scientific fields.
method: The editorial describes three colloquia that cover the observatory's achievements in planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
result: The paper highlights the revolutionary impact of Arecibo across multiple disciplines.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has left a lasting legacy in planetary science, astronomy, and geospace research.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This colloquium reviews the scientific legacy of planetary radar observations at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids.
result: Arecibo's planetary radar was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, enabling detailed characterization of many Solar System objects.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system made significant contributions to planetary science, and its loss marks the end of an era for ground-based radar astronomy.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper is a historical review of radio astronomy contributions from the Arecibo 305-m telescope, covering pulsars, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave background detection.
motivation: To document the scientific legacy of the Arecibo Observatory after its collapse, highlighting its impact on radio astronomy and related fields.
method: The paper provides a historical perspective, summarizing key scientific achievements enabled by successive upgrades of the Arecibo telescope.
result: Arecibo made influential contributions to pulsar studies, neutral hydrogen mapping, interstellar medium characterization, VLBI imaging, SETI, and the first detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.
conclusion: Arecibo's legacy in radio astronomy is enduring, with its major upgrades continuously expanding observational capabilities and scientific impact over five decades.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews geospace science advances achieved with the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere and ionosphere are highlighted, aiming to summarize key scientific contributions.
method: The paper is a colloquium review, synthesizing results from incoherent scatter radar, lidar, and optical measurements at Arecibo.
result: It covers advances in plasma physics, space weather, atomic metal layers, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in geospace research, and the review underscores its legacy and scientific impact.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The authors review experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of convection-cloud chambers that reproduce key cloud phenomena under controlled conditions.
result: Convection-cloud chambers can capture essential processes like turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentration and supersaturation, bridging laboratory and atmospheric scales.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to address the precipitation bottleneck, but the paper does not contribute to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from neutrino-driven core collapse supernovae and their detection methods.
motivation: Observing a Galactic core collapse supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, providing insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.
method: The paper summarizes recent progress in core collapse supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection and parameter estimation methods for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the latest modeling results and signal predictions, along with detection strategies for multimessenger observations.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from core collapse supernovae, combined with photon and neutrino observations, will offer unique insights into the supernova central engine and neutron star formation.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on large-scale structure surveys.
motivation: The cosmological principle is a foundational assumption of the standard ΛCDM model; testing its validity is crucial for cosmology.
method: The authors analyze dipole anisotropies in radio galaxy and quasar catalogs and compare them with the cosmic microwave background dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the matter dipole and the CMB dipole, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may indicate new physics beyond ΛCDM, but systematic effects need further investigation.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews astrophysical tests of self-interacting dark matter, focusing on dark matter halo dynamics and large-scale structure.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and test models where dark matter particles self-interact, which could explain small-scale structure observations.
method: The review synthesizes observational constraints from galaxies to large-scale structures, comparing predictions of self-interacting dark matter models with data.
result: The paper summarizes current astrophysical bounds on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and discusses future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable model, and upcoming surveys will provide more stringent tests.

title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, but recent experimental results have constrained its parameter space. The paper aims to survey the current status and future discovery potential.
method: The authors review theoretical developments and experimental constraints, then project the discovery potential of the HL-LHC across multiple search channels and well-motivated scenarios.
result: The paper provides an overview of viable supersymmetric models and estimates of the HL-LHC's sensitivity to them.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable in certain scenarios, and the HL-LHC will significantly extend the search reach.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion and neutrino production.
motivation: To advance understanding of hydrogen-burning nuclear reactions in stars, which is crucial for predicting stellar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work over the last decade on nuclear reactions, plasma and atomic physics in the solar environment.
result: Updated understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning and its implications for solar models.
conclusion: The review summarizes progress in solar fusion research but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding gas bubble dynamics is important for many natural and industrial processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The paper is a review summarizing key advances over the past 20 years in bubble dynamics, including experimental and modeling approaches.
result: It highlights the effects of turbulence, non-Newtonian rheology, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The review provides insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems, but has no relevance to quantum information theory or related fields.

Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

tldr: This paper reviews the nonlinear elasticity theory of buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with applications in materials science and biology.
